clue.text: (& 24dn.) "Blasted civilians, getting in the way of US war aims," according to Pentagon?

definitions.text: "Blasted civilians, getting in the way of US war aims," according to Pentagon?

blocks.clueFragment: Blasted civilians, getting in the way of US war aims
blocks.note: read straight, a bitter description of innocent people killed because they stood near a military target
the setter's reading: this is the bloodless euphemism the US military itself uses for such deaths

explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks and 'according to Pentagon' tell you to find the official jargon, not a plain description. Private Eye's satire is aimed at how the phrase softens killing.
explanation.definitionFit: The military euphemism names unintended civilian casualties and property destruction caused incidentally by an attack on a legitimate target.

clue.text: Clinton's first affair (female abandoned) rocked the land

indicators.note: what comes first in a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
something abandoned is left behind, so those letters are dropped from the word
rocked means shaken about, so the letters are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: the opening letter of the former President's name
taken as written
F is the standard abbreviation for female; one of the two Fs goes

explanation.surface: A scandal over Bill Clinton's first fling that shook America.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points at the Lewinsky scandal shaking the nation, but 'rocked' is the anagram signal and 'the land' is a whole continent. Drop one F from AFFAIR, add C, and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Africa is a continent, a vast landmass, so the setter can call it a land in a loose geographical sense.

clue.text: Self-conceit: can Sir Dicky miss out?

indicators.note: dicky is British slang for shaky or unsound, so the letters around it are not in working order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, taken as written
more anagram fodder

explanation.surface: Wondering whether some knight called Dicky could bear to be left out of the honours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sir Dicky' looks like a name, as in Sir Richard Attenborough, but 'Dicky' is the instruction and splits the fodder. 'Out' just rounds off the surface question.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive admiration of oneself is a direct synonym for vanity or conceit, named after the youth in Greek myth who loved his reflection.

clue.text: Embrace, taking drugs and sit round university

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: E is ecstasy, so more than one is ES
to sit for a portrait is to pose
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone taking drugs and loafing around a campus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Embrace' looks physical, but here it means to adopt a cause. The U sits inside POSE, after the drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: To espouse a belief or cause is to adopt and support it, the figurative sense of taking something to your heart.

clue.text: Wearing Obama's underpants? Almost (not to go on about it)

definitions.text: not to go on about it

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: you are 'in' the clothes you wear
in American English, which the President speaks, underpants are shorts

explanation.surface: A tabloid question about what the President has on under his trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Obama is there to make the underwear American: in US usage 'shorts' can mean underpants. Lose the last letter and you have the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is used to sum things up briefly, cutting a long story down without dwelling on detail.

clue.text: see 22ac.
Hit externally, Left reeling from declared policy of standing party

indicators.note: something acting externally is on the outside, so it surrounds another piece
reeling means staggering about, so the letters lurch out of order

blocks.note: to pat is to hit lightly
standard abbreviation
anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: The political Left staggering after a blow from an election rival's manifesto.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From' looks like a link to the definition, but it is the anagram fodder. A 'standing' party is one standing for election.
explanation.definitionFit: A party's manifesto of stated principles and pledges put to voters at an election is called its platform.

clue.text: see 25ac.
Screwing Daffy Duck takes seconds? Not when you're in top form

definitions.text: Not when you're in top form
definitions.note: the definition describes the times as a clause; the answer is a plural noun for them

indicators.note: screwing twists something round and round, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, shaped like O
anagram fodder
standard abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: A crude image of a quick fling with the cartoon Daffy Duck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Daffy Duck' reads as one cartoon character, but the words split: Daffy is fodder and Duck gives O. In cricket, being out for a duck means scoring zero.
explanation.definitionFit: An off day is a bad day when you perform below your usual standard, the opposite of peak condition.

clue.text: Volume produced on turning over girl with Vaseline initially inserted

indicators.note: turning something over flips it end to end, so the letters run backwards
initially means at the start, so only the opening letter counts
something inserted is put inside, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: taken as written
the opening letter of the brand of petroleum jelly
a girl's name

explanation.surface: Private Eye smut about turning a girl over with the help of Vaseline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' reads as loudness in this surface, but it means a book. 'On turning over' also sounds sexual, yet it only tells you to reverse a two-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: A short novel is a single book, and a volume is a word for any one bound book.

clue.text: Colin Powell at last moving to back Bush's end, leaves little to the imagination

definitions.note: the definition is a verb phrase describing the garment; the answer is a noun

indicators.note: at last means at the very end, so only the final letter is kept
moving means shifting position, so the letters change places
going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run backwards
an end is the final part, so only the closing letter counts

blocks.note: the final letter of the general's surname
anagram fodder
taken as written
the final letter of the President's surname

explanation.surface: Colin Powell finally switching to support George Bush, a move that hides nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue splits 'Colin Powell' so that the first name is fodder and the surname gives its last letter. Powell was Bush's Secretary of State.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrap of cloth wrapped around the hips covers very little of the body, so it barely conceals anything.

clue.text: Posh, extremely randy, squeezing zit – head to rear!

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two outer letters, so only those are kept
sending the head to the rear moves the front letter to the back
squeezing something means pressing it between two sides, so one piece holds the other

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word meaning lustful
a zit is a pimple

explanation.surface: A lustful posh person squeezing a spot, with an exclamation to turn around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posh' might suggest Posh Spice, but it is the definition, in the British sense of upper-class and smart. 'Head to rear' moves only one letter, not the whole word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritzy means luxurious and fashionable, from the grand Ritz hotels, which is what posh means in British usage.

clue.text: (& 15ac.) Bollocks: drops one to get naked

blocks.note: teardrops, so drops of water from the eye
a means one, as in 'a pound'
to remove all your clothes

explanation.surface: An exclamation of disbelief at someone dropping a garment to strip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bollocks' looks like the exclamation 'nonsense!', but here it is the British verb 'to bollock', meaning to reprimand harshly. The colon hides that it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, to bollock someone is to give them a severe scolding, which is exactly what tearing a strip off them means.

clue.text: The soft option for violent inmates?

definitions.text: The soft option for violent inmates?

blocks.note: read straight, a lenient punishment for prisoners who cause trouble
the setter's reading: a literally soft room where patients liable to hurt themselves are confined

explanation.walkthrough: 'Soft option' is an idiom for the easy choice, but the setter means soft to the touch. 'Inmates' can be asylum patients as well as prisoners.
explanation.definitionFit: Asylums used rooms lined with cushioning to stop disturbed patients from injuring themselves, literally soft surroundings for dangerous occupants.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Taking head of financier's shoulder, I ran riot

indicators.note: the head of a word is its top, so only the opening letter is taken
a riot is wild disorder, so the letters are thrown into chaos

blocks.note: the opening letter of the money man's title
anagram fodder, taken as written

explanation.surface: A banker grabbing someone by the shoulder before running wild.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ran riot' does double duty: it is the definition, and 'riot' also tells you to jumble the letters before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Plants that flourished grew luxuriantly and spread unchecked, which is the gardening sense of running riot.

clue.text: Spiritual guide's talk: "get end away"

indicators.note: getting the end away means removing the tail, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: British slang: to rabbit, from rhyming slang 'rabbit and pork', is to chatter

explanation.surface: A clergyman's sermon urging the congregation to have sex, 'get your end away' being British slang for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Get your end away' is crude British slang for having sex, and here it literally drops the end of the word. Rabbit comes from Cockney rhyming slang 'rabbit and pork', talk.
explanation.definitionFit: A Jewish religious teacher and leader of a congregation is a spiritual guide for its members.

clue.text: Lofty's on crack – great chance of being a star?

definitions.text: great chance of being a star?

blocks.note: lofty means tall
a crack is a break

explanation.surface: A tall man nicknamed Lofty taking crack cocaine, hoping for stardom.
explanation.walkthrough: Lofty reads as a nickname and crack as the drug. In a down clue 'on' means placed above, so the first piece sits on top of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: An entertainer's first major opportunity that leads to fame is known idiomatically by this phrase.

clue.text: Dope ring after mum

indicators.note: after means following, so one piece comes behind the other

blocks.note: mum as in 'keep mum', silent
a ring is round like the letter O

explanation.surface: A drugs ring operating after someone's mother.
explanation.walkthrough: Mum looks like mother, but it is the adjective meaning silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal insults for a stupid person, so they are slang synonyms.

clue.text: Critic's a tit

blocks.note: someone who knocks, or runs things down
vulgar slang for a woman's breast

explanation.walkthrough: The surface calls a critic an idiot, which is the obvious sense of 'tit'. The setter instead wants its slang sense of breast.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who constantly disparages is a knocker, and in vulgar British slang breasts are also called knockers.

clue.text: "Cyclops's jams," said spiritual types

indicators.note: said means spoken out loud, so the words are judged by their sound

blocks.note: the setter's own jams, 'jams' meaning sticks fast

explanation.surface: The setter complaining about his own jams, quoted by a group of spiritual people.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters often use their own name for 'my' or 'me'. Jam here is the verb meaning to become stuck, not preserves.
explanation.definitionFit: People who seek union with the divine through contemplation and inner experience are spiritual by nature.

clue.text: (& 6dn.) Roger to get this, say, in Beau's embrace

definitions.note: the definition is a verb phrase whose object is the answer: to roger is to get one's leg over

indicators.note: an embrace wraps arms around someone, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: a beau is a boyfriend or lover
e.g., 'for example', is what 'say' means in 'a fruit, say'

explanation.surface: Someone called Roger hoping for a cuddle from his boyfriend.
explanation.walkthrough: Roger reads as a man's name; here it is British slang for having sex. 'Getting your leg over' is the equally crude British idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang, to roger someone and to get your leg over both mean having sexual intercourse, so the idioms match.

clue.text: Banker maybe, ready to stand by Labour's leader (one who's finished)

indicators.note: a leader goes at the front, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: the ready is British slang for cash
the opening letter of the party's name
someone who ends a thing

explanation.surface: A banker ready to back the Labour leader, perhaps a politician whose career is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' looks like an adjective but is the noun: 'the ready' is British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: A bank is one kind of business that lends funds at interest, so a banker is an example of this.

clue.text: see 1dn.
(& 8dn.) Source of support for Obama? Not Hillary for some time

blocks.note: Michelle Obama, the President's wife
Hillary Clinton held the role until 2001

explanation.walkthrough: In 2009 Hillary Clinton was Obama's Secretary of State, so she might look like his source of support. The title she once held has gone to his wife.
explanation.definitionFit: The title belongs to the wife of the American President, which Michelle was then and Hillary had been years earlier.

clue.text: "F — legislation!" – Verity

blocks.note: taken as written
an Act of Parliament is a piece of legislation

explanation.surface: Someone called Verity swearing at a new law, with the expletive printed as F and a dash.
explanation.walkthrough: Verity looks like the name of the speaker, and the F and dash look like a censored swear word. The F is just a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Verity is a literary word for truth, and something true or known to be the case is a fact.

clue.text: Not the full frontal Camilla's powder

indicators.note: not the full thing means only part of it, so the answer is a stretch inside the words

blocks.note: runs across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A glimpse of Camilla, Prince Charles's wife, not quite naked, with some powder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Full frontal' pulls together as a phrase about nudity, but 'Not the full' is the instruction and the answer spans the break between the two names.
explanation.definitionFit: Talcum is a soft mineral ground fine and dusted on skin, the everyday example of a body powder.

clue.text: A toothy thing recruited by whips, remains underground here

indicators.note: someone recruited is taken into a group, so one piece is drawn inside the other

blocks.note: a cat o' nine tails is a whip
taken as written
a comb has teeth

explanation.surface: Someone with big teeth taken on by the party whips, who remain below ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Whips suggests the parliamentary enforcers who recruit members. Here they are cats, short for cat o' nine tails.
explanation.definitionFit: Underground galleries in which the dead were buried are places where human bones and bodies still lie.

clue.text: Hailer broadcast started by Conservative twit

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, as seed is, so the letters are spread into a new order
started by means having something at the front, so one piece leads

blocks.note: standard abbreviation
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A loudhailer announcement made by a foolish Tory.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a charlie is a fool, as in 'a proper charlie'. It can also mean cocaine, which the Eye would enjoy.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are mild British insults for a silly or foolish person, making them slang synonyms.

clue.text: Crapper's first loo exploited good north eastern toilet water

indicators.note: what comes first is at the front, so only the opening letter is kept
something exploited has been worked over, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the opening letter of the plumber's name
anagram fodder
standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Thomas Crapper's first lavatory making use of a good flushing water supply in the North East.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Crapper was a Victorian plumber linked with the flush toilet, so the lavatory surface fits. 'Toilet water' sounds like a cistern but is the perfume term.
explanation.definitionFit: Eau de toilette, a light perfume, translates literally from French as toilet water, and eau de Cologne is its classic example.
